title: The Holy Family
hook: the Sunday after Christmas honors an ordinary family life

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Holy Innocents, and a mother who would not be comforted. Your line was rachel weeping. Which child or place stayed with you? Day six hundred forty-three.

Between the infant in the manger and the grown man at the Jordan, Luke gives one scene. Jesus is twelve. The family goes up to Jerusalem for Passover with a crowd of relatives, and on the way home Mary and Joseph realize, a full day's walk out, that he isn't with the cousins. Three days of searching follow. On the Sunday after Christmas, the Church sets aside the angels and the star and looks at a family, worried, tired, and very ordinary.
screen: `TWELVE YEARS OLD.` → `LOST ON THE WAY HOME.` → `THREE DAYS OF SEARCHING.`

segments.voice: They find him in the temple, sitting among the teachers, listening and asking questions. Mary says: your father and I have been searching for you, sorrowing. And he answers that they should have known he must be about his Father's business. Luke says they didn't understand. Then comes the sentence the whole feast leans on. In the Douay-Rheims: "And he went down with them, and came to Nazareth, and was subject to them." Subject to them. The one John called the Word that made all things goes home and does what his parents tell him. And then Luke folds every year until he is about thirty into one line: "And Jesus advanced in wisdom, and age, and grace with God and men." That's almost everything we know. Mark's gospel calls him the carpenter, using a Greek word that means a builder or craftsman. The Gospels are silent about the rest: no stories of his teenage years, his friends, the day Joseph died. Tradition fills the silence with what Catholics call the hidden life, the long years at Nazareth of work, meals, prayer and village life. In today's calendar the feast of the Holy Family is kept on the Sunday after Christmas. The point isn't that this family was perfect. Luke shows them anxious, confused, and misunderstanding each other. The point is that most of the years Luke counts were spent at Nazareth, among relatives, at ordinary work. Catholics see in that a dignity for every family's daily life, the dishes included.
screen: `FOUND IN THE TEMPLE.` · `HE WENT DOWN, AND WAS SUBJECT.` · `THE QUIET YEARS IN ONE LINE.` · `THE HIDDEN LIFE AT NAZARETH.` · then, large: `AN ORDINARY FAMILY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pick one family chore and plan to do it gladly. The one you usually sigh at: dishes, laundry, taking out the trash, calling a relative you owe a call. Sit, and picture doing it slowly and without complaint, maybe even without being asked. Picture the faces of the people you share a home or a life with. Families come in many shapes; yours counts. If you pray, you can offer the chore for them. If you don't, simply hold them in mind. The bell holds the time.
The Holy Family. Jesus, Mary and Joseph, honored on the Sunday after Christmas for an ordinary family life at Nazareth. Today's word.
Your line: an ordinary family. Today, do the chore you chose, gladly, and see if anyone notices. Day six hundred forty-three.

howItsDone: Catholics keep the feast of the Holy Family on the Sunday within the octave of Christmas (or on December 30 when there is no such Sunday), and some parishes bless families or renew marriage vows that day.

fork.reveal: he answers that they should have known he'd be about his Father's business. then he goes home with them and is subject to them.

original.note: Greek: a builder or craftsman, Mark 6:3's word for Jesus, usually rendered carpenter.

trapdoor: what you thought: the Holy Family was a perfect family.
what it means: Luke shows them anxious and confused; the feast honors the ordinary life Jesus lived at Nazareth.
what a scholar hears: Luke 2:51–52 covers the years until he is about thirty (3:23); tektōn in Mark 6:3 means builder or craftsman.

notes: 'About eighteen years' derived from age twelve (Luke 2:42) and 'about thirty' (Luke 3:23). Confirm framing.
Feast extended to the universal Church by Benedict XV in 1921; moved to the Sunday within the Christmas octave in 1969. Confirm.

The finding in the temple (Luke 2:41–52) is the gospel in Year C only; Years A and B use other infancy passages. The hook says 'the only story the Gospels tell between infancy and adulthood', which is accurate for the canonical Gospels.
The death of Joseph is not recorded in the Gospels; stated as silence.

Editor review (2026-10-01): fork and teach now follow Douay-Rheims Luke 2:49 ('about my Father's business'); 'eighteen years' replaced by Luke's 'about thirty'; 1921/1969 dates cut and myth item replaced; 'only story' and parent-feeling lines cut.
